title: A Classroom Management Strategy Every Teacher Should Use eacher-should-use/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin presents the 'do it again' strategy as a superior alternative to the two common but ineffective teacher responses when students perform a routine procedure poorly: ignoring it, or reacting with visible frustration and a lecture. The strategy simply has students repeat the procedure correctly, delivered without added negative commentary, since students already understand why they're redoing it and don't benefit from being told what they did wrong. He cautions that inconsistent use of the strategy — letting a poorly done procedure slide even once — undoes prior teaching, and lays out five precise steps for applying it: waiting for full attention before speaking, stating simply that the procedure was done incorrectly, giving a calm one-sentence instruction for the redo, staying silent until it's completed, and acknowledging success or repeating the cycle if needed. He frames brevity and unemotional consistency as the strategy's core strengths.
points: The 'do it again' strategy corrects procedural failures without lecturing, which preserves the student relationship while still holding a standard.
Letting even one poorly executed procedure slide undoes the effect of prior teaching and invites recurring failure.
The five-step process relies on waiting for full attention, a single calm instruction, and silence until the redo is complete.
Brevity and unemotional consistency, not volume or explanation, are what make the strategy effective.
quotes: The former will result in more of the same behavior from students and an eventual loss of control (see article on broken windows theory). And the latter, when repeated often enough, will cause private resentment and make classroom management an uphill battle.
The fact is, students understand why they have to do it again and don’t benefit from the teacher spelling it out for them.
If your students perform a procedure incorrectly or inappropriately and you let it pass without a response, even one time, you’ll undo the work you did teaching the procedure in the first place.
Effective classroom management requires an unbending commitment to respond every time expectations aren’t met.
Students respond more favorably to actions and clear, concise speech. The “do it again” strategy fits this definition perfectly.
